About: sliding vs toppling on a slowly tilting rough ramp

Source

Concept
Explores when each of three differently proportioned blocks on a slowly tilting rough ramp first moves, and what decides whether that first motion is a slide or a topple.
Serves
JEE / NCERT Class 11 mechanics — static friction and toppling of rigid bodies.
Inquiry
Raise the ramp slowly, watch each block for its first sign of motion, and compare what you observe across different friction settings.
Misconception
Puts common intuitions about heavier and larger blocks to the test — the cards let you commit to a prediction and then watch what actually happens.

Pedagogy principles applied

Predict before revealEach of the six cards commits a prediction before the ramp is tilted or a threshold curve is shown.
Target the misconceptionDistractors encode "heavier slides sooner / bigger holds longer"; the sim withholds masses so every such intuition must be tested, not assumed.
What is invariantThe cards ask which observed quantities stay the same across blocks and which depend on shape — the inset chart collects the evidence one failure at a time.
Operational numberstan θ and μₛ are read live; the plumb line through each COM shows where the vertical falls relative to the block's base as the ramp tilts.
Formal layer on demandThe theory curve and sliding line stay hidden until the student has found them through the cards.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Question 1

The three blocks are drawn without their masses being given, and the simulation offers no way to set them. Before raising the ramp, predict how the angle at which a given block starts to slide would change if that block were twice as heavy.

2 · Question 2

Set the friction slider to its default μ_s = 0.5. Before raising the ramp, predict which block moves first and what it does.

3 · Question 3

Leave μ_s = 0.5 and keep tilting past the first failure. Before doing so, predict how the medium block and the cube give way.

4 · Question 4

Before trying other friction settings, predict what single comparison decides whether a given block slides first or topples first.

5 · Question 5

Now set μ_s = 0.7. Before raising the ramp, predict what the medium block does this time.

6 · Question 6

The friction slider runs from 0.2 to 0.8. Before searching, predict whether any setting of it can make the cube topple.

The Physics

Slide or topple · what it is about, the physics behind it, and what every control does

A ramp tilts, slowly, from level. The cube starts on it; the medium block and the tall block wait in the table until you drag them on. Two sliders set the angle and the grip — and the masses are never given to you, because you will not need them.

1What you'll work out

  • Whether a heavier block gives way sooner than a lighter one — and why the sim can refuse to tell you any masses at all.
  • What decides which block moves first, and what decides how it moves: by sliding, or by tipping over.
  • Which of the two thresholds friction can change, and which one it cannot touch at all.

JEE / NCERT Class 11 — static friction, equilibrium of rigid bodies, and toppling about an edge.

2What this simulation shows

A ramp hinged at one end is raised steadily from level. Three blocks share the same width — one a cube, one medium, one tall — and the cube is the one that starts on the ramp. Drag either of the others on from the table when you want it in the run. The surface under every block you place is identical, and its grip is yours to set.

As the ramp rises, each block reaches a point where it can no longer stay put. Watch for the first sign of movement — the angle it happens at, and whether the block slips down the slope or tips forward over its lower edge. Those are two different failures with two different causes.

Nobody told you the masses — and you don't need them. Both ways of failing lose their mass in the same cancellation.

01

Why can the sim withhold the masses?

Sliding: the pull down the slope and the friction that resists it are both proportional to m.
Toppling: both torques about the corner carry the same mg, so it divides out here too.
  • Down the slope the weight supplies mg sin θ; friction can supply at most μsmg cos θ. Set them equal and m cancels: sliding begins at tan θ = μs.
  • About the downhill corner the righting torque is mg·(w/2)cos θ and the tipping torque is mg·(h/2)sin θ. Same cancellation: tipping begins at tan θ = w/h.
  • So "the heavier block goes first" is not a near-miss — mass does not appear in either threshold. Doubling a block's mass changes nothing at all.
02

What is actually happening at the moment it tips?

The medium block (w/h = 0.6667) below and at its toppling threshold. The dashed line is the plumb line through the centre of mass; the grey ring is the corner it would pivot about.
  • The normal force is not stuck at the middle of the base. As the ramp tilts, it slides downhill by xN = (h/2)tan θ to keep the block in balance.
  • It can only go as far as the corner. Once xN would need to exceed w/2, there is no balance left and the block goes over.
  • That is the same statement as "the plumb line through the COM leaves the base" — which is what the sim draws.
The offset, and the exact moment it runs out of base.
03

One comparison decides everything

Two thresholds, and the block does whichever comes first as the ramp rises.
Both thresholds are a tan θ, so comparing them is just comparing μs with w/h.
  • Friction sets one sliding angle shared by all three blocks; shape sets three different toppling angles that friction never touches.
  • A block slides if μs < w/h and topples if μs > w/h. Nothing else enters.
04

Reading the whole story off one chart

The sim's inset, computed: one rising cyan line for sliding, three flat lines for toppling. Every crossover sits at μs = w/h.
  • The toppling lines are flat — rub the ramp with oil or glue and a block's tipping angle does not move by a degree.
  • The tall block's line is crossed already at μs = 0.40, so at the default 0.50 it is past its crossover and topples.
  • The medium block crosses at μs = 0.6667: it slides below that and topples above. This is exactly why it behaves differently at 0.50 and at 0.70.
  • The cube's line is at 45°, needing μs > 1. The slider stops at 0.80, so within this sim the cube can only ever slide.
Why one of the six cards has "no" for an answer.
05

The three blocks, side by side

Each block drawn at its own first-motion angle, at the sim's default μs = 0.50.
The full table: three shape ratios, three toppling angles, one shared sliding angle.
  • The medium block and the cube let go at the same 26.57°, even though one is half again as tall — because at μs = 0.50 both are sliding, and sliding does not care about shape.
  • The tall block goes earliest of the three, at 21.80° — not because it is heaviest, but because it is the narrowest relative to its height.
  • Change μs and the order can change. Change the masses and nothing changes.
06

The traps they'll set for you

  • "The heavier block slides at a smaller angle." Mass cancels on both sides of mg sin θ = μsmg cos θ. Same angle, every time.
  • "Rougher ramp, so it topples later." Backwards. Roughness delays sliding, which can leave toppling as the thing that happens first — a rougher ramp makes toppling more likely, not less. The tipping angle itself never moves.
  • "The big block has more friction because it has more surface." The friction limit is μsN, and N does not depend on contact area. The cube and the tall block share the same sliding angle exactly.
  • "It topples because the ramp pushes it over." Nothing pushes. The normal force simply runs out of base to act on, and the weight's own line of action falls outside the corner.
  • "Somewhere in 0.2–0.8 the cube must topple too." It needs μs > 1. The answer to that card is genuinely no.
07

Ninety-second self-test

At μs = 0.50 the medium block and the cube both go at 26.57°. Make the cube out of lead. What changes?

Nothing. 26.57° = arctan 0.50 contains no mass, no size and no material — only the friction coefficient. Both blocks still let go at exactly the same angle.

A block is 3 cm wide and 4 cm tall. At what μs does it switch from sliding first to toppling first?

At μs = w/h = 0.75. Below that it slides (arctan μs < arctan 0.75 = 36.87°); above it, arctan μs is the larger angle, so the 36.87° toppling threshold arrives first.

Why does the tall block's first-motion angle stay at 21.80° whatever you do to the friction slider?

Because at every setting on the slider (0.20 to 0.80) it is already past its crossover at μs = 0.40 for most of the range — and once toppling is the earlier threshold, the angle is arctan(w/h) = 21.80°, a pure geometry number. Only below μs = 0.40 does the sliding line drop underneath it, and there the angle does move.

You want a block that never topples on any ramp, however rough. What shape?

Any block with w ≥ h, so that w/h ≥ 1 and toppling would need tan θ ≥ 1, i.e. θ ≥ 45°. Below 45° it can only slide. (Strictly, it could still topple on a ramp steeper than 45° — the cube's own line in the chart.)
